newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil soybean ending stocks seen negative-Safras.
newsitem.headline: Brazil soybean ending stocks seen negative-Safras.

text.p: Brazil will not be able to meet soybean export and crushing commitments in the next six months with ending stocks likely to slip into negative territory, independent consultant Safras e Mercado said.

Soybean stocks were 9.25 million tonnes on August 1, down 15 percent from the same period last year, and ending stocks for the 1997/98 marketing year (February/January) were seen to show a deficit of 454,000 tonnes, Safras said in a weekly report.

"The origin of this disequilibrium is the excessive volume of soybean sales for export," it added. Brazil has exported 6.40 million tonnes since February, a jump of 127 percent over the same period last year.

July exports totalled 1.58 million tonnes, up from 1.27 million tonnes in June and from 469,000 tonnes in July 1996. The Netherlands bought 765,000 tonnes, Japan 117,000 tonnes, China 103,000 tonnes and the United States 101,000 tonnes.
Export registrations to July 31 indicate Brazil still has to load an extra 2.29 million tonnes, which would invariably involve importing more than currently forecast, Safras said.

"Sales cancellations must really take place and be high, following the market modification (a considerable drop in prices) and the difficulty exporters are having obtaining soybeans and meeting existing commitments," it added.

Additional imports would have to come mainly from the United States since no soybeans were available in Argentina. This would involve higher freight costs and a 10 percent import tax which does not apply to partners in the Mercosur customs union.

Imports were 134,000 tonnes in July, up from 120,000 tonnes in June and 99,000 tonnes in July 1996. Between January and July, Brazil imported 610,000 tonnes of which 551,000 tonnes were from Paraguay and 58,000 from the United States.
"These volumes should start to grow especially after October, when the first cargoes of the new U.S. harvest are expected to arrive," Safras said.

Crushing was estimated at 11.39 million tonnes by August 1, just one percent lower than during the same period in 1996, based on data from the Brazilian Association of Vegetable Oils Industries (Abiove).
This was likely to be the least flexible component of demand and low stocks will keep internal prices high, regardless of what happens on the Chicago commodities futures market, Safras predicted.
